title: Other Marine Structures
analyses: Wave loading and wave impact analysis
Coastal hydrodynamic and wave transformation analysis
Sliding, overturning and foundation bearing analysis
Seabed scour and sediment transport analysis
Flooding, hydrostatic pressure and buoyancy analysis
Local impact and accidental loading analysis
scope: Applicable to breakwaters, seawalls, offshore bridges, coastal protection structures, intake structures, outfalls and offshore towers.

models.text: The suite should implement the continuity equation, conservation of momentum, Bernoulli's equation, Euler fluid equations, Navier–Stokes equations, hydrostatic pressure equations, Archimedes' buoyancy principle, classical elasticity, beam and plate theories, limit equilibrium, sliding resistance and overturning stability formulations.

The suite should include Airy linear wave theory, Stokes higher-order wave theory, cnoidal wave theory, solitary wave theory, Boussinesq equations, nonlinear shallow-water equations, mild-slope wave equations, spectral wave action conservation, wave shoaling, refraction, diffraction, reflection and breaking models. Advanced methods should incorporate Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, Reynolds stress models, standard and realizable k–epsilon turbulence models, k–omega SST models, large-eddy simulation, volume-of-fluid free-surface tracking, level-set methods and coupled wave–structure interaction.

models.group: Overtopping, armour and coastal protection models
models.text: The suite should include Hunt's wave run-up relationships, Iribarren surf similarity parameter formulations, EurOtop overtopping prediction methods, Hudson armour stability relationships, Van der Meer armour stability models, rubble-mound breakwater stability models, porous-media flow models and wave-induced pore-pressure response.

Models should include Shields sediment initiation, Meyer–Peter–Müller bed-load transport, Engelund–Hansen sediment transport, Van Rijn transport relationships, Exner sediment continuity, suspended sediment advection–diffusion equations, erosion–deposition flux models and morphodynamic seabed evolution.

The suite should employ Terzaghi bearing capacity, Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, consolidation, Darcy seepage, Bishop slope stability methods, Morgenstern–Price limit equilibrium, finite-element soil models, seismic response formulations, S–N fatigue analysis, corrosion models and fracture mechanics.

These should include coupled wave–sediment–morphology models, CFD–structural interaction, wave–seabed poromechanics, hydrodynamic–geotechnical coupling, mesh-based and meshless free-surface simulations, coastal digital twins, data-assimilated wave forecasts and uncertainty-aware coastal protection optimization.

inputs.text: Breakwater crest elevation, slope, armour layer thickness, seawall dimensions, bridge span, pier geometry, intake/outfall alignment, foundation dimensions and structural cross-sections.
Seabed elevation grids, shoreline profiles, water depths, nearshore slopes, coastal topography and channel geometry.
Offshore wave spectra, significant wave height, peak period, wave direction, extreme wave heights and wave transformation conditions.
Water-level time series, tidal constituents, current velocities, storm surge, long-period water-level variation and discharge flow rates.
Sediment grain-size distribution, density, porosity, fall velocity, critical shear stress and sediment mobility characteristics.
Soil stratigraphy, shear strength, foundation stiffness, bearing resistance, permeability and settlement characteristics.
Concrete properties, armour rock density, rock grading, steel characteristics, geotextile properties and material durability.
Wave impact, hydrostatic pressure, uplift, earth pressure, vessel impact, debris loading and traffic loading.
Base friction, embedment depth, groundwater pressure, drainage characteristics and existing foundation geometry.
Offshore wave boundaries, tidal boundaries, river inflows, outfall discharges and coastal sediment supply.
Sea-level-rise scenarios, corrosion conditions, abrasion rates, storm frequencies and exposure duration.
Allowable overtopping, flood protection elevations, structural displacement limits and required design service life.

subtitle: Breakwaters, seawalls, offshore bridges, coastal protection structures, intake/outfall structures and offshore towers.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the existing or proposed geometry of the marine structure and its surrounding seabed or coastal terrain. These shall include structural elevations, slopes, wall thicknesses, armour layers, bridge supports, intake and outfall configurations and the initial seabed profile.

For coastal hydrodynamic analysis, the initial state shall specify water-surface elevation, flow velocities, water depth and, where necessary, initial wave conditions across the computational domain. Sediment-transport analyses shall initialize seabed elevations, sediment composition, bed roughness and suspended sediment concentrations.

For breakwaters and seawalls, the initial structural condition shall include the as-placed armour arrangement, foundation condition, backfill state, pore-water pressure and any existing settlement or displacement. For bridge and tower structures, the initial state shall include gravity-induced stresses and existing support conditions.

Flooding simulations shall start with a defined water level and initial flooded or dry condition in each relevant region. Erosion and long-term deterioration studies shall begin with measured or specified initial damage, corrosion, foundation exposure and sediment conditions.
bc: At offshore hydrodynamic boundaries, incoming wave spectra, wave elevation histories, wave direction and appropriate wave-generation or wave-absorption conditions shall be prescribed. Open-water boundaries shall allow outgoing disturbances without artificial reflection as far as practicable.

Coastal and shoreline boundaries shall represent impermeable walls, permeable armour, overtopping, wave run-up, seepage and friction according to the physical structure. River mouths, intake systems and outfalls shall use prescribed inflow rates, discharge velocities, pressure conditions or receiving-water levels.

At the seabed, the model shall apply bed roughness, bottom friction, sediment entrainment and deposition conditions. Soil-foundation boundaries shall represent bearing support, friction, uplift, seepage and geotechnical deformation.

Structural boundaries shall prescribe gravity, hydrostatic pressure, hydrodynamic impact, wave uplift, traffic loading and vessel collision where applicable. Seismic analysis shall apply ground-motion histories through the foundation.
For overtopping and flooding studies, downstream boundaries shall permit water discharge, accumulation or return flow according to the surrounding terrain and hydraulic conditions.

calibration: Calibration should use wave-flume experiments, coastal wave-basin measurements, bathymetric surveys, sediment transport experiments, hydrodynamic field monitoring and structural load testing.
Wave transformation parameters should be calibrated using measured wave heights, periods, directions, breaking locations and nearshore water levels.
Wave run-up and overtopping parameters should be calibrated against physical-model experiments for representative slopes, crest elevations, roughness and armour arrangements.
Breakwater armour stability models should be informed by measured armour displacement, rock grading, hydraulic loading and laboratory failure observations.
Seabed scour and sediment transport models should be calibrated using sediment grain-size measurements, bed shear stress observations, sediment flux measurements and repeated bathymetric surveys.
Foundation parameters should be calibrated using soil investigations, direct shear tests, bearing experiments and settlement observations.
For coastal intake and outfall structures, flow resistance, discharge mixing and relevant hydraulic coefficients should be calibrated using hydraulic laboratory tests and field velocity measurements.
Flooding and coastal inundation parameters should be informed by measured water levels, flood extents and documented extreme events.
verification: Wave transformation and coastal hydrodynamic models should undergo benchmark tests covering wave propagation, reflection, refraction, diffraction, shoaling and wave breaking within the scope of the chosen formulations.
Spatial resolution, temporal resolution, boundary reflections and numerical wave-energy dissipation should be assessed through systematic convergence studies.
Overtopping and run-up implementations should be checked against established reference test cases and independently calculated benchmark solutions.
Sediment transport and seabed evolution models should be verified through sediment conservation checks, equilibrium bed tests, transport-direction tests and mesh sensitivity.
Structural stability calculations should be checked using independent sliding, overturning, buoyancy, bearing and hydrostatic loading benchmarks.
Structural finite-element models should undergo stress and displacement convergence studies, including local impact and fatigue-sensitive regions.
Flooding calculations should be checked for water-volume conservation, boundary condition correctness and consistency between inflow, outflow and stored water.
Coupled hydraulic–structural and seabed–foundation simulations should be checked for consistent transfer of pressures, loads, erosion depths and support reactions.
validation: Wave height, wave direction and breaking predictions should be compared with independent field measurements or controlled laboratory wave-basin datasets.
Run-up and overtopping predictions should be validated using physical experiments and, where appropriate, monitored coastal structures during storms.
Breakwater stability should be assessed against independent physical-model tests and documented armour displacement following extreme sea states.
Scour and sediment transport predictions should be compared against measured bathymetric change and sediment movement.
Seawall and coastal structure loading should be validated using pressure sensors, structural strain measurements and experimental wave impact records.
Hydraulic performance of intake and outfall structures should be assessed against measured velocities, discharge characteristics and relevant field observations.
Flooding and inundation predictions should be evaluated using independently recorded flood levels and surveyed flood extents.
Structural deterioration and reliability predictions should be compared with inspection records and observed damage over time.

geometry.text: Breakwaters, seawalls, revetments, coastal protection structures, offshore bridges, offshore towers, submarine intake structures, outfalls, submerged culverts and marine hydraulic structures.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, IFC, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for seawall cross-sections, breakwater armour geometry, bridge structures, intake/outfall chambers, submerged conduits, foundations and hydraulic equipment.

geometry.cat: Civil, coastal and geospatial geometry formats
geometry.text: LandXML, InfraGML, CityGML, GML, GeoPackage, GeoJSON (.geojson), ESRI Shapefile (.shp with supporting files), GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, XYZ and NetCDF (.nc) with defined spatial coordinates should be supported for coastlines, bathymetry, topography, breakwater alignments, shoreline boundaries and coastal terrain. InfraGML provides standardized encodings for several land and infrastructure geometry concepts, including alignments and surveys.

Gmsh MSH, CGNS, SU2 (.su2), Fluent-compatible MSH where the reader is implemented, OpenFOAM polyMesh directory structures, VTK/VTU, MED, Exodus, and UGRID-compliant NetCDF meshes should be accepted for suitable coastal-flow, wave-transformation and hydraulic calculations. Nastran BDF and Abaqus INP can support structural and foundation models.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, LAS/LAZ, E57, XYZ point clouds, multibeam bathymetry and photogrammetric coastal meshes should be supported for irregular breakwater armour, erosion profiles, scour holes, seabed obstacles, cliffs and damaged marine structures. Raw bathymetric soundings must be transformed into consistent computational surfaces or meshes before analysis.
